title: Saving for College with Compound Interest
learningObjectives: Understand how time and compound interest can increase savings
Understand the value of starting early to save for post-secondary education

sources.title: Saving for post-secondary education (teacher guide) — Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Building Blocks activities

Information created by the CFPB is in the public domain. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has not reviewed, approved or endorsed this activity.

evidence.quote: Compound interest is when you earn interest on both the money you save and the interest you earn.
The sooner you start saving in an account that pays interest, the faster your money can grow.

explanations.text: Compound interest means you earn interest on both the money you save and the interest you already earned, so starting early in an account that pays interest helps money grow faster.

evidence.quote: So let's say you invest $1,000 (your principal) and it earns 5 percent (interest rate) once a year (the compounding frequency).
The second year, you would have $1,102.50.

explanations.text: A $1,000 principal earning 5 percent once a year shows compounding frequency in action, reaching $1,102.50 in the second year because interest is earned on the prior balance.

evidence.quote: Increasing the compounding frequency or your interest rate or adding to your principal can help your savings grow even faster.
Interest can be compounded annually (once each year), semi-annually (twice each year), monthly, or daily.

explanations.text: Increasing the compounding frequency, interest rate, or principal can help savings grow even faster, and compounding can happen annually, semi-annually, monthly, or daily.

predictions.prompt: You save $1,000 at 5% compounded yearly for 10 years for education costs. What is the amount after 10 years?
